questions.question: Which idea means that the people themselves are the source of all government power?
questions.correctAnswer: Popular sovereignty
distractors: Divine right
Judicial review
Nullification
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty is the opening claim of the Constitution itself: 'We the People' ordain it. Governments in the American system hold only the power citizens grant them, which is why elections and constitutions limit officials.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: We the People - power starts with the people, not the officeholders.

questions.question: The Preamble to the US Constitution begins with which three words?
questions.correctAnswer: We the People
distractors: Four score and
In order to
When in the course
questions.explanation: Those three words announce that the Constitution's authority comes from citizens rather than from a king or from the states alone. The rest of the Preamble lists the government's purposes, from forming a more perfect union to securing liberty.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: We the People - three words that locate all authority.

questions.question: Americans replaced the Articles of Confederation with the Constitution mainly because the Articles:
questions.correctAnswer: Left the national government too weak - it could not tax, regulate interstate trade, or enforce its laws
distractors: Gave the president unlimited power over the states
Created a national court system that was too strong
Required states to abolish their own governments
questions.explanation: Under the Articles, Congress begged states for money and could not stop trade wars between them. Shays' Rebellion and unpaid war debts convinced leaders in 1787 that a stronger federal frame was necessary.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No tax power, no trade power - the Articles starved the union.

questions.question: The Federalist Papers were written to accomplish what goal?
questions.correctAnswer: Persuade New Yorkers - and the public generally - to ratify the new Constitution
distractors: Defend the Articles of Confederation against change
Campaign for the election of George Washington
Explain the text of the Bill of Rights after ratification
questions.explanation: Hamilton, Madison, and Jay published 85 essays under the name Publius arguing that the proposed union could protect liberty better than the loose confederation. Federalist No. 10 and No. 51 remain classic statements on factions and separated powers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Publius argued for ratification - 85 essays for the Constitution.

questions.question: James Madison's answer in Federalist No. 10 to the danger of factions was that:
questions.correctAnswer: A large republic controls faction best, because so many competing interests make an oppressive majority hard to assemble
distractors: Factions disappear when government bans political parties
A small republic controls faction best through close supervision
Factions should be given their own branch of government
questions.explanation: Madison argued you cannot remove faction without destroying liberty itself, so you must control its effects. Extending the republic multiplies interests and sects, forcing coalitions to bargain rather than letting one majority faction rule unchecked.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: More interests, less faction danger - Madison's big-republic remedy.

questions.question: Under federalism, powers that belong only to the national government, such as coining money and declaring war, are called:
questions.correctAnswer: Enumerated (delegated) powers
distractors: Reserved powers
Concurrent powers
Implied liberties
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 8 lists Congress's enumerated powers, from taxation to war. Powers not granted to the nation nor denied to the states are reserved to the states or the people by the Tenth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Listed in Article I - enumerated powers belong to the nation.

questions.question: A state runs its own public schools while the federal government also funds education programs. Education is therefore best classified as what kind of power in practice?
questions.correctAnswer: A shared field where states hold primary, reserved authority and the federal government acts through spending and civil rights law
distractors: An enumerated federal power listed in Article I
A power denied to both levels of government
An exclusively local power with no state role
questions.explanation: The Constitution never mentions education, so the Tenth Amendment leaves it to the states, which delegate operations to local districts. Washington influences schools through funding conditions and by enforcing rights such as those in Brown v. Board of Education.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Schools are state-run; Washington enters through money and rights.

questions.question: The Supreme Court's ruling in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) strengthened federal power by holding that:
questions.correctAnswer: Congress may use implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause, and states may not tax federal operations
distractors: States may tax federal banks if rates are reasonable
Congress has only the powers expressly listed in the Constitution
The Bank of the United States was unconstitutional
questions.explanation: Chief Justice Marshall reasoned that a power to create a bank follows from the taxing, borrowing, and commerce powers, and that state taxation of the bank would let states destroy a federal instrument. The case remains the foundation of implied-powers doctrine.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: McCulloch - implied powers are real, and states cannot tax the nation.

questions.question: The Bill of Rights - the Constitution's core charter of individual freedoms - consists of:
questions.correctAnswer: The first ten amendments, ratified together in 1791
distractors: The first five amendments, ratified in 1789
All 27 amendments, ratified in 1791
The last ten amendments, ratified in 1868
questions.explanation: Voters and states demanded a written rights charter as the price of ratification, and James Madison shepherded twelve proposed amendments through Congress; states ratified ten of them by December 1791. Seventeen further amendments followed over the next two centuries, bringing the total to 27.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten amendments in 1791 - the Bill of Rights was ratification's price.

questions.question: Which path correctly states how the US Constitution is formally amended?
questions.correctAnswer: Proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention) and ratification by three-fourths of the states
distractors: Proposal by the president and approval by a national referendum
Proposal by a majority of state governors and approval by the Supreme Court
Proposal by two-thirds of the Senate and signature by the president
questions.explanation: Article V makes amendment deliberately hard, which is why only 27 have succeeded. Every successful amendment so far was proposed by Congress; states ratify through legislatures or conventions as Congress directs.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths ratify - Article V sets a high bar.

questions.question: The First Amendment protects which set of freedoms?
questions.correctAnswer: Religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
distractors: Speech, arms, and protection from searches
Religion, jury trial, and bail
Press, arms, and quartering protection
questions.explanation: The First Amendment's five freedoms are the core of American civic expression. Courts protect even unpopular speech, while allowing limits such as true threats and incitement to imminent lawless action under Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms in the First - religion, speech, press, assembly, petition.

questions.question: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court protected students' free speech by ruling that:
questions.correctAnswer: Students do not shed their First Amendment rights at the schoolhouse gate, absent substantial disruption
distractors: Students have no speech rights while on school property
Schools may ban any symbol they dislike for any reason
Student newspapers may never be regulated in any way
questions.explanation: Mary Beth Tinker wore a black armband protesting the Vietnam War. The Court sided with the students because the school showed no evidence of disruption, setting the standard Louisiana students still rely on today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rights do not stop at the schoolhouse gate - Tinker.

questions.question: The Fourth Amendment protects Americans primarily against:
questions.correctAnswer: Unreasonable searches and seizures, generally requiring warrants based on probable cause
distractors: All searches by police under any circumstances
Self-incrimination in criminal cases
Excessive bail and cruel punishments
questions.explanation: The amendment grew from anger at British writs of assistance - general search warrants. Modern exceptions exist, such as consent, plain view, and searches incident to arrest, but the warrant-and-probable-cause rule remains the default.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no probable cause, no search - the Fourth Amendment default.

questions.question: A defendant who 'takes the Fifth' is using the Fifth Amendment's protection against self-incrimination, which means the defendant:
questions.correctAnswer: Cannot be compelled to testify against himself or herself in a criminal case
distractors: Never has to appear in court at all
Cannot be tried in a state court
Must be released without bail in every case
questions.explanation: The right to remain silent, reinforced by Miranda warnings after arrest, keeps the burden of proof on the government. The same amendment also guarantees due process and just compensation when government takes private property.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fifth lets you stay silent - the state must prove its case.

questions.question: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) required states to provide:
questions.correctAnswer: A free attorney to criminal defendants who cannot afford one, under the Sixth Amendment as applied by the Fourteenth
distractors: Free bail for all defendants awaiting trial
A jury of twelve in every civil case
Automatic appeals for every conviction
questions.explanation: Clarence Gideon, tried without counsel in Florida, petitioned the Supreme Court in pencil from prison. The unanimous ruling made appointed counsel a basic condition of a fair trial in felony cases, later extended to any case risking imprisonment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gideon - no money for a lawyer does not mean no lawyer.

questions.question: The Fourteenth Amendment transformed the Bill of Rights through the process called selective incorporation, meaning:
questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court applied most Bill of Rights protections against state governments, one right at a time, through the Due Process Clause
distractors: States incorporated their own bills of rights into federal law
Congress incorporated state laws into the Constitution
The Bill of Rights automatically applied to states in 1791
questions.explanation: Originally the Bill of Rights limited only the federal government (Barron v. Baltimore, 1833). After 1868, cases from Gitlow (1925) onward incorporated nearly every major protection against the states - the reason a Louisiana arrest follows the same Miranda rules as a federal one.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fourteenth carried the Bill of Rights into every statehouse and parish court.

questions.question: The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments are known together as the:
questions.correctAnswer: Reconstruction Amendments
distractors: Progressive Amendments
Bill of Rights
Prohibition Amendments
questions.explanation: Adopted between 1865 and 1870, they abolished slavery, defined citizenship and equal protection, and barred denying the vote because of race. Together they rewrote the Constitution's relationship to freedom after the Civil War.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 13, 14, 15 - freedom, citizenship, vote: the Reconstruction Amendments.

questions.question: The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) changed American democracy by:
questions.correctAnswer: Prohibiting denial of the vote on account of sex, enfranchising women nationwide

Abolishing poll taxes in federal elections
Giving women the right to own property
questions.explanation: Generations of suffragists, from Seneca Falls in 1848 to the pickets of the 1910s, won ratification in 1920. Louisiana ratified symbolically decades later, in 1970, long after Louisiana women were already voting under the amendment's force.

questions.question: A Louisiana citizen who is 20 years old is protected in voting by which amendment if a state tried to set its voting age at 21?
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-sixth Amendment, which sets the voting age at 18
distractors: The Fifteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1971 during the Vietnam era, the Twenty-sixth Amendment answered the slogan 'old enough to fight, old enough to vote.' It binds both state and federal elections, so no state may set an age above 18 for voting eligibility.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 18 to vote, coast to coast - the Twenty-sixth Amendment.

questions.question: The Twenty-fourth Amendment and the Harper v. Virginia decision together eliminated poll taxes by:
questions.correctAnswer: Banning them in federal elections by amendment (1964) and in state elections by Supreme Court ruling (1966) under equal protection
distractors: Repealing them through an act of Congress in 1960
Persuading states to repeal them voluntarily by 1950
Replacing them with literacy tests nationwide
questions.explanation: Poll taxes had disfranchised poor Black and white Southerners for decades - a central tool of Louisiana's 1898 constitution. The amendment-plus-litigation sequence shows the two different routes by which voting barriers fell in the 1960s.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Amendment killed the federal poll tax; Harper killed the state one.

questions.question: Article I of the Constitution creates which branch, and what is its primary job?
questions.correctAnswer: The legislative branch - Congress - whose job is to make the laws
distractors: The executive branch, whose job is to enforce the laws
The judicial branch, whose job is to interpret the laws
The military branch, whose job is to defend the nation
questions.explanation: Congress is placed first in the Constitution because the framers saw lawmaking as the people's branch. Its two chambers, the House and Senate, must both pass a bill in identical form before it can become law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article I, Congress first - the lawmaking branch.

questions.question: Members of the US House of Representatives are apportioned among the states by population and serve terms of:
questions.correctAnswer: Two years, with all 435 seats up for election every two years
distractors: Four years, with half the seats up every two years
Six years, with a third of the seats up every two years
Life terms after appointment by state legislatures
questions.explanation: Short House terms keep representatives close to their districts, while the Senate's six-year terms insulate senators somewhat from daily opinion. Reapportionment after each census shifts House seats among states - Louisiana currently holds six House seats.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House: 435 seats, two-year terms, always close to the voters.

questions.question: The Senate's constitutional role in the appointment process is to:
questions.correctAnswer: Advise and consent - confirming or rejecting the president's nominees for cabinet posts, judgeships, and ambassadorships
distractors: Nominate candidates for the president to consider
Approve state governors' appointments
Write the job descriptions for federal judges
questions.explanation: The framers split appointments: the president nominates, the Senate confirms by majority vote. Louisiana's two senators vote on every federal judge and cabinet secretary, one reason Senate elections carry national weight.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: President nominates, Senate confirms - advise and consent.

questions.question: A bill passes both houses but the president neither signs nor vetoes it while Congress adjourns within ten days. The result is:
questions.correctAnswer: A pocket veto - the bill dies without becoming law and cannot be overridden
distractors: The bill becomes law automatically
The bill returns to the Supreme Court for review
The bill becomes law but only for one year
questions.explanation: The presentment clause gives the president ten days (Sundays excepted). If Congress is in session and the president does nothing, the bill becomes law; if Congress has adjourned, inaction kills it - the pocket veto, immune to override because there is no veto message to reconsider.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Adjourned Congress plus silence equals pocket veto - no override possible.

questions.question: Congress can override a presidential veto only by:
questions.correctAnswer: A two-thirds vote of both the House and the Senate
distractors: A simple majority vote of the Senate alone
A vote of three-fourths of the state legislatures
A ruling of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Overrides are rare because assembling two-thirds in both chambers requires broad bipartisan agreement. The override power is the clearest example of checks and balances running from Congress back toward the president.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds in both houses beats a veto - checks run both ways.

questions.correctAnswer: Impeachment

Filibuster
Censure by the Senate
questions.explanation: The House impeaches by majority vote - the equivalent of an indictment. The Senate then holds the trial, and conviction and removal require two-thirds of the Senate; for a president, the chief justice presides.

questions.correctAnswer: Most legislation effectively needs 60 votes for cloture to end debate, giving a determined minority blocking power not mentioned in the Constitution

The Constitution requires 60 votes for all Senate bills
Debate can never be limited on any measure in the Senate

questions.question: The president's primary constitutional role is to:
questions.correctAnswer: Enforce and execute the laws as head of the executive branch
distractors: Write laws for Congress to pass
Interpret laws for the courts
Serve as chief justice of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Article II vests 'the executive Power' in the president, who heads the cabinet departments and federal agencies. Presidents also serve as commander in chief and chief diplomat, but lawmaking itself stays with Congress.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article II enforces - the president executes the laws Congress writes.

questions.question: To become president, the Constitution requires a person to be:
questions.correctAnswer: A natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States for at least 14 years
distractors: A citizen for at least 10 years and at least 30 years old
A natural-born citizen and at least 40 years old
A resident of one state for at least 20 years
questions.explanation: These are among the very few qualifications the Constitution sets for federal office, and neither Congress nor the states may add to them. The same natural-born rule applies to the vice president, who must also be eligible to serve.

questions.question: The Electoral College decides presidential elections such that a candidate must win:
questions.correctAnswer: 270 of the 538 electoral votes - a majority of the whole college
distractors: A majority of the national popular vote
All votes in at least 26 states
Two-thirds of the electoral votes
questions.explanation: Each state gets electors equal to its congressional delegation; the District of Columbia gets three under the Twenty-third Amendment. Louisiana casts 8 electoral votes. Winning the popular vote without 270 loses the election, as happened in 2000 and 2016.

questions.question: Suppose the Electoral College finishes with no candidate holding a majority of its votes. Under the Twelfth Amendment, the choice of president then falls to:
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives, voting by state delegation, choosing among the top three candidates
distractors: The Senate, voting by individual members
The Supreme Court, choosing the popular-vote winner
A new national election held within 60 days
questions.explanation: This contingent election has happened twice, in 1800 and 1824. Each state delegation casts one vote - Louisiana's six representatives must agree internally to cast the state's single vote - and 26 states are needed to elect.

questions.question: A president orders agencies not to spend money Congress has appropriated for a program he opposes - a practice called impoundment. Under the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974, the president:
questions.correctAnswer: May not unilaterally impound the funds; a proposed rescission takes effect only if Congress approves it within the statutory window
distractors: May impound any funds for any reason as commander in chief
May impound funds permanently if the Senate is out of session
May impound funds unless two-thirds of the House objects
questions.explanation: Nixon-era impoundments provoked the 1974 act, and in Train v. City of New York (1975) the Supreme Court ordered funds released even under earlier law. The episode is a leading example of Congress reclaiming its Article I power of the purse against executive overreach.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The purse belongs to Congress - a president cannot pocket-veto spending by silence.

questions.question: As commander in chief, the president heads which institution?
questions.correctAnswer: The armed forces of the United States
distractors: The National Guard of every state at all times
The United Nations peacekeeping forces
State police forces during emergencies

Collecting tariffs on imported goods

Cancel elections in districts they dislike
Choose who is allowed to vote in each district
questions.explanation: Equal population alone does not guarantee fair maps, which is why courts and commissions argue over compactness, parish splits, and communities of interest. Louisiana's maps have been challenged under both the Constitution and the Voting Rights Act on exactly these grounds (standard C.11j).

questions.question: Louisiana's capital was not always Baton Rouge. The capital moved from New Orleans to Baton Rouge in 1849 mainly because:
questions.correctAnswer: Leaders wanted a capital farther from New Orleans' distractions and influence - and Baton Rouge's bluffs offered a healthier, defensible site
distractors: New Orleans was destroyed by fire that year
Baton Rouge was the largest city in the state
The federal government ordered the move in 1849
questions.explanation: The capital wandered afterward - to Opelousas and Shreveport during the Civil War - before settling permanently in Baton Rouge in 1882. Huey Long's 1932 tower, still the nation's tallest capitol, fixed the city's status in stone (standard C.9i context).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Out of New Orleans' shadow, onto Baton Rouge's bluff - 1849.

questions.question: Louisiana elects its governor to a term of how many years, with a limit of how many consecutive terms?
questions.correctAnswer: Four-year terms, limited to two consecutive terms
distractors: Two-year terms with no limit
Six-year terms limited to one
Four-year terms with no limit
questions.explanation: The two-term limit came by constitutional amendment in the 1960s, though a former governor may run again after sitting out. Governors share executive power with several separately elected officials, such as the lieutenant governor and attorney general - a plural executive.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four years, twice in a row at most - Louisiana's governor rule.

questions.question: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, to:
questions.correctAnswer: The states respectively, or to the people
distractors: The president
The Supreme Court
The federal bureaucracy
questions.explanation: The amendment was the Anti-Federalists' price for ratification: a written guarantee that the new national government was one of enumerated powers. It is the constitutional home of state authority over schools, elections administration, and parish government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Not granted means reserved - the Tenth Amendment's plain deal.

questions.question: The Commerce Clause became one of Congress's most powerful tools because courts read 'commerce among the several states' to include:
questions.correctAnswer: Activities that substantially affect interstate commerce, even if they occur inside one state
distractors: Only the physical shipment of goods across state lines
Only trade with foreign nations
Only commerce conducted by water
questions.explanation: From Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) through the New Deal cases, the clause supported laws on railroads, labor, civil rights, and environmental protection. Cases in the 1990s and 2012 health care litigation reminded Congress the power still has judicially enforced limits.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Affect interstate commerce and Congress may reach it - with limits.

questions.question: Article III creates the Supreme Court and leaves the rest of the federal court system to:
questions.correctAnswer: Congress, which established the district courts and courts of appeals - including the Fifth Circuit that covers Louisiana
distractors: The president acting alone
State legislatures in each circuit
The chief justice's personal discretion
questions.explanation: There are 94 district courts and 13 courts of appeals. Louisiana sits in the Fifth Circuit, headquartered in New Orleans, whose rulings bind federal courts in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas unless the Supreme Court reverses them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One court in the text; Congress built the rest - Louisiana answers to the Fifth.
